When he was General of to brigade he en- tailed the ceneure of the great Napoleon, al hough the latter admired him for hie genius and bravery. The Emiwror, in me of his characteristic fits of passion, deprived him of his command, telling him he Amid never again draw a mord in the mmice of France. POPI. lAN Sunset ton FIELD Or 11..—At the Wilts and Rugs Agri. ultural College, recently, • very interesting and instructive lecture AVM delivered by Prof. W. Frerim, F. 0.8., on the sot oject of ls Grasses and Han." The lecture was characterintic of the style of teaching adopted at the College, the whole of it being given and illustrated in the water meadow adjoining the Cullege.—Prof. Fream mid that the special feature of the College being the teaching of science as connected with and having a direct beariug on the practice of agriculture, he had seized the opportunity presented by the commencement of the hay harvest to draw the attention of the students to various impormot points connected with the crop they' had assembled to help to gather in. He would first remind them that their water meadow. bordering the river Avon were fed elf by eheep down to the end of April, eo that the luxuriant swathes which they now eon falling before the scythe were the re. tale of only two menthe' growth during the favourable weather which had attended the past season. They most not leave out of amount, however, the valuahle manurial effect be to the grazing of over IMO sheep ; nor must they forget that the meadows, intersected as they were M every diredtion by water carriers, had been periulically flooded. The heterogeneous character of the plants in the hayfield wm noted, and it was estimated that there were come forty different grasses reg melded The grasses differed indefls nitely in appearance, habit, and time of dowering. Thee had already hem or familiar with the characters by which they wme able to distinguish between the various gram., both hut and gnarl. By good grames he meant those that were of undoubted dietetic value, and which it was desirable to encourage ire every possible way. The bad or weed gra eee, on the other hand, were such or from various rea- sons should he discouraged as much as pomible, though their inferiority sem due to various mums. Thus the eoft grass. alio called honey ~TllB9, and Yorkshire fog, speci- mens of which they would see here and there around them, was by no means deficient in herbage; yet it was a very litter and unpalatable gram, no much eu that whea it wes very plentiful it was found necessary ,to add salt to the boy to induce horses to eat it. In some of the nonlsern cnunties he had seen fields consisting at- meet entirely of thie undesirable grans, and through lune- ranee of the varied character of greases it wan allowed to !flourieh without cheek, there being, he feared, • very preys- lent notion among fartnere that one gram was as good as another, though this was one of the most unfortunate con- ceptions that ever took posseesion of the bucolic mind. Other grams., again, such as the hair gram, which they saw erowing on the Tv:nalne of the meadows, and the equally common quaking gram, were by no mmes devoid of nutriment, but their Lthit was too sparse and their herbege too smety Cu make them valuable fodder grasses or hay plants. Yet others, such so barley greases, for which he was glad to say the soil of those meadows was too etiff and moist, and the small reed gram, were decidedly objection- able became of their sharp, brittle awns, whkh pierced and irritated the milieu of the animals that ate them. Poimn- one grasses, like the darnel, were fortunately net common, and he did not feel sorry that he had been unable to find them a single growing specimen on the College Farm. After pointing out tlmt the proper time to cut gram was when the majority of the grames in a field were in full flower, end that in making hay the gram simply lost about 55 per cent. or BS per cent. of its own weight of water, he went on to show the amount of injory to the proepeetive hay; from interruptions by rain entirely depended on the waylin which they turned it during the time of curing. Ifs showed them that growing gramee were coverest with a thin coating of waxy matkr, which every noticeable in cermle, mpeci.dly wheat, and this was really a waterproof coat with which the grange furnished themselvm. If in turning and tending the gram they ueed it gently and not violently, the waterproof coat would not get broken, no that any rain that fell daring the first few daye would do no harm, as it would simply moisten the outside of the prostrate plants, hut would net penetrate into and wash out the valuable and nutritiom constituent., After the lecture the students and professors etripped to their shirk, rolled up their sleeves, and proceeded with the actual work of hay-making.

, Rex P POCITV. —The fact i 3 that Free Trade favours and ' Protection hampers production. The Free Trade nation obtains more of what it consumes for the amount of “stored work" it pays away than does the Protectionist nation. And much of what it consumes of food and raw material is a direct energiser of its productive capacity. The bounty fed" sugar of Prance underselling Bristol sugar in the Eng- Rah market, raises all workmen's wages throughout Eng- land. But the tax on English Won 'entering Germany lowers all workmen's wages throughout Germany. A day', labour will purchase four pounds of sugar at fkl. per lb.; but it will purchase eight pounds of sugar, ad, per lb. A day's labour will purchase nor hammer for Is. 111, but it will purchase two if iron is so cheap that haunners can be made at half that price. Again, Free Trade increases in- definitely the area of supply, and no the steady income and reliable quality of .ill the roanufacturers'and the consumers' needs. It is only if we omit to notice the fact that Free Trade favoum and Protection hampers the proper activity of productive industry that we can bring ounselvm even to face the itueetion of discussing Protection in the some breath with Free Trade. . . . The ' ' "

question is, indeed, much discussed under the plea of the introduction of Reciprocity. What, then, is the nature of this Reciprocity—this substi- tote thee is proposed as the efficient, because the only pos- sible, means of securing all the advantagm attainable in a Free Trade direction, when Free Trade itself can only be one-sided ? Its supporters, in common with all advocates of the application of any theory, lay claim to the title of common sense for their theory. If common sense be any- thing awes than an unmeaning name, it is that natural sagacity which combines fact and theory aright: conse- quently, to my of a theory that it is a common-sense theory 13 to assert of it that it join true accord with right practice. Duties imposed for purrases of Reciprocity discriminate between articles of foreign and home production, for the express and avowed purpose of fostering the home produc- Con. But there are two types of Reciprocity. The one type is a naked evil it simply seeks to save from the natural and wholesome doom of open competition some industry dart hae shown itself inferior to that of the foreigner. This ie simply to establish a poor.rate for the support of certain unprofitible workers. The citizens at large contribute from their fear I-won profits to make up the deficiencies of a few of their number, who are devoting their energies to work that does rot" piv." The other type has much more plausi- bility on its curt roe—in is based on the argument that when a foreign country gives to its own producers unnatural ad- vantages, men must take some means to counteract the evil effeetsof t!,saction outsiderson their home production. Bat this is to ignore the fact that such unnatural advantages,: and they are sm.-idly designated unnatural, must in the end bring uptu themselves thew own destruction. And this destructitn must come upon them with greater speed then! the indirect effect of their competition on industries flourish- , ing under truer or more natural conditions. Such is the un- doubted Ittic of the question and such Itts been the teach- ing of experience. The thinking community wilt notice the exisdente of hostile tariffs, but it will say with Carlyle— en Htswile tariffs may arise and shut us out, but they will fall sod let us in." Tunes of commercial depression teach the worthlemnem of proteetesl industry by the fact of the far more intense distress which prevails in land. velure trotee- tinri mire than in Via., presided over by Free Trade. MI sotboriLies set down the ilktreas in England from 1t039-12 as ten times greater than that mffored in the commercial de- pression in 1,77-ft. And there is no doubt bet that policies of restriction raise prices and curtail supplies, while more liberal policies have an exactly opposite emult ; and low prices end abundance of gapplies are the main instincts to the alleviation of commercial depression—. BISHOP BRAS. ON JCSTIFIABLB Woes—ln the course of a sermon to the men el the 4th Staffordshire Ride Volun- teers, at their encampment, Oxley Manor, on Sunday evening, the Bishop of Manchester said The motto of the volunteers is" Defence, not defiance." It that motto were always remembered in England and amongst nations, then woold wars almcst tease throughout the world. At en,' rate that motto we were rather fond of trumpeting somo! years ago ought to have taught the English people that the wars which have too often shed a false halo of glory around nations have been unjust, short-siditel, selfish, unjustifiable , were l an,l that there are only two just apologies for any war , either that it wae a war of sell-defence. or that it was under-1 taken to prevent, not a remote.possible, indefinite, inuminary danger, but an actual, pressing, and imminent great wrong. I will take two instances trots our own history, and not flout any reo.nt period of tl. for fear I should be thought to be stimulating She political passions of the do'. The resis- tance to the Spanish Armada was a war of self-defence, and the assistance that Elizabeth sent to those Protestants of the Low Countries who under Alva and the Inquisition were suffering intolerable tyranny both of body and mind. and if ever there was a just cause in which a nation should un- sheath a sword, it was the cause that shed the blood of Philip Sidney on the field of Zutphen. If all the wars in which this country had lv-en engaged were as pure as these, England's annals would not have been one whit leas glorious than they are.

The bread fruit tree, artocarpus incise, grows to the height of about 40 feet. It is from 1 foot to 15 inches in diameter the bark io fish.coloured, full of little chinks,and covered bY small knots; the inner bark is throne, lire good emooth, soft, and of a yellow colour. The branches coine out in a horiaontal manner, about 10 feet trove the ground, and beeotue shorter as they near the top. The leave. are divided into? or Alobes, about 18 inches or 2 feet long, and are of a lively green. The tree bears male and female Bowers, the males among the upper leave., and the females at the extremeties of the twigs. When full grown the fruit is about 9 inches long, heart shaped, of a greenish co/our, marked with h.sagoiral warts formed int. tacit.. The pulp is white, partly farinaceous and partly fibrous; bat whetl quite ripe becomes yellow and juicy. The whole treeorhan in a green state, abounda with a viscid milky juice, of no tenacious a nature or to he drawn into threads. It continnes productive for about eight months in the year. The earliest account of it is by Captain (bumpier, in 1088. It was originally found in the eastern parts of Asia, and the islands of the Pacific,arol was brought to England try Captain thigh, in August, 1703. This in abstracted from Blonds History of the Veget.ible Kingdom. The banana (muss, sapientum) is sometimes cap.t the bread fruit tree. "'
EvwAnn (imam, Warrington.

I suppose " Delta's" question refers to the fruit tree of Ceylon, which the natives coil" Dehgaba:' It grows as high as the jack tree, and has very large branches, which, twice sneer, in March and June, are hung with round rough tfnit, about the !MP of an infant's heady The fruit is everywhere used, both by natives and Europeans, as an article of food. When boilf d t resembles a potato, but is more watery. It is often cut into slices and fried, in which state it is very crisp. The wood, which is white and rather course, is not much used. The leavea are large and of a dark green. The fruit grows from the ends of srnall branches, and does not rise inunediately from the trunk as the j,a fruit does. There is, however, another tree of the sanie species, called the foreign bread fruit tree (rata-del-gahs). its 1,1‘,1 are not so large as those of the common bread fruit, and are not unshed. The fruit ice thick ofvl, about sin inches long, and when split contains a, number of white seeds, as Lig as peas. These are eaten he the natives when boiled. This tree is much need for making canoes, its trunk being frequently long, straight, and thick, and the wood light and durable. J. Haunts, St. Helens.

For the enbghtenment of "Ignorance ' let me say that Since the abolition of the Irish Parliament in MI there bae been only one Parliament for the Government of the three kingdom, of England, Ireland, and brooked. The bringing of Ireland tinder the rule of the English Parliament I, always spoken of as "The onion." This union necessi- tated an alteration in the national banner. Thin banner wen Cllll,l a "Jack" hy the sailors in the time of James I, who nniten England and Scotland, and it was no called be- cause of the name Jacques, that of the king, being inscribed upon it. When The union took piano" the banner had three crosses put upon it, one being St. George's crosn for England, one Of. Andrew's cross for Scotland, and the third St. Patrick's for Ireland. This was the reason why the ban- ner was ever afterwards called the Union Jack..
L. 8., Altrincham.

The reason this runner woe called the Union Jack woo owing to the union of Kn.land and Scotland in the reign of James the let., the creole of St. George being placed upon the crow. of St. Andrew. The flog was then called the " Union Jack," "Jacque " being the Latin word for Ja.nes. J. S., Stoke-on.l.rent.

"J. L. D." has been rightly informed that a barrister can- not maintain an action for hie fees. The duties of a barrister are expected to be considered by the vulgar heard outside the profession as honorary, and doe fees he pockets not., payment for him but es a gratuity. If be seem to demand fees be would be regard.' as having done among to his repu- tation. This is, of course, simply "blarney" in the estiTna. lion of any bonnets, man. A barrister will refuse brief if he suspect, that there to not the slightest -chance of getting his fee, but he invariably refuses to trust to chance. If he flmen't ask for the fee himself his clerk in usually pretty lively io looking after it when the brief, presented, and before a single stroke of work is done by the "learned gentleman," sf, that the whole thing resolves itself into a veritable piece of humbug. A junior barrister never expects to receive less than five guineas ion once, and a Q.C., would commit a breach of barristers' trade unionism if he under- tOOk CaSe fee less than ten guineas, except it WAS done at the clirect ion of a judge when a criminal not up a plea of for. 4 pauperism. If "J. L. D." thinks he can .diddle" a barrister out of his fes of terre ten guineas, if the latter makes • moll of a ease and an Amor himself, be is sadly out of hie reckoning. The barriater works on the ready-money system; he doesn't chalk up any client', debts, hence one never hears of a barrister suing for his fees. This, I believe, I, the true state of affairs. slit linen I should like some correspondent to ray. R. M. D., Warrington.

Bann, of marriage are solemn notices of matrimonial contracts, made in the parish-church before marriage; that if there he any objections to either party as to prior engage- ments, ic, there may be an opportunity of making them. The publication of beans, popularly called asking in the church, was intended to prevent clandestine marriages; lett a licence man be obtained fur the marriage, and then this ceremony is omitted: hut miuistera ate cotta celebrate matrimony between any pernons without a licence, except the banns have been Bret published three several times, upon pain of suspension, kn. The net of matrimonial banns is said to have been first intraluced in the Gallicao church, thon,gh something like it obtained even in the primitive times: and it in this that Tertullian is supposed to mean by trimundina prornulgatio. The council of Lateran first extended and made the usage general. By the ordinance Of Blois, no person could validly contract marriage, with- out a preceding pruclamatien of three benne mu' cOuld any person whatever he exempt except for the two last.

—AFt/HAN AFFAIRS. A 'C.:Stage bee been received at Quettah from colonel St. John, at Candahar, reporting that the prepratione for de- ' fence am proceeding satisfactorily. The " country people," who were supposed to be friendly to mr, have attacked our working parties. The neighbourhood of the citadel haa been cleared as far as possible, and "the entire Pathan popu- lation" hoe I,en expehed or left the city voluntarily. The lows in the defeat at Kuelik-i-Nakhad are again re- turned at 1,100 out of 2,800 men engaged. The 66:h and the Bombay Grenadiers lost their colours in the battle, and ,it is stated that most of the officers of the British regiment were killed in defending the colour/. From Cabot there is news of the ribng of the tribesmen in Maiden and Warrilk. What General Roberts expects, and is no doubt prepered to ! meet, is a repetition of the tacticeof the Afghan force which en nearly overthrew General Stewartbi coition, at Ahmed hey]. General Robert/ marched from Cobol for Candahar on Sundly. . .

--ST;."—Tuesday. A despatch from Candahar dated the 6th net,i announces that the measures taken to place the city in. state of defence are now completed, and there is a supply of provisions, except forage, for 35 days. The lows sustained by General Burrows's force were exag- gerated in the first reports. They do not exceed a 1000 men, of whom 400 are Europeans and 21 officers. The Wall Shore Ali beat Candahar. Ayoub Khan's force is very large, but at present in an undisciplined condition. Snake, Wedneeday.—Cabul news to the Io,h reports the Ameer moving to Itch Knjak, three miles front Shirpur, with sirdars and chiefs, and that the majority of the tribesmen bare been tent to their home. The Ameer comes to Shirpur on the Ilth to meet General Stewart, who, after the inter- view, follows the troops to Butkak, the first march from Cabal. R-ports from General Roberfence favourable. The Ghilzai country and Northern Afganistan are quiet. Quettah reports a letter received from Candahar, dated sth. The garrison have abundant weer, food, and ammunition. A telegram from Simla, dated Thursday. sly, that the news from the columns marching to the relief of Candahar it satisfactory. Sir I). Stewart effected the withdrawal of I all the troops front Cabal on Wednewlay "in admirable order and perfect tranquility," and proceeded as far as But- kak on his way to Gandamak. The Atreer came to Cahill in the morning nn a vieit to Sir Donald Stewart and Mr. Lepel Griffin before their departure. Ile is said to have favourably impressed all the English °dicers, and to have exprepacd his gratitude to the British tiovernment in "dignified language." A private telegram from Quettah Rays that the progress in the arrangements for the advance on Candahar is satisfactory. All the troops are in high spirits, and eager for the order to proceed. The Beloocheee, who have hitherto refused to cross the frontier, are now carrying stores for us over the Khojak Pass,stid assisting on to the extent of their power.

CONSTAIMNOPLF. Sunday. The Sultan to-day gave orders to Hussein Ilusni Pasha, the Minister of War, to leave for Dulcigno on the 11th inst. with 2,000 troops. The Minister has promised to transfer the district to Montenegro within the time stipulated for its surrender, and the town itself e few days later. With regard to the Turco-Greek question the Sultan has directed a proposal to be drawn up torn precise frontier line, which will be submitted to the Powers. An smicahle solution of the question is expected. The Council of Ministem held a further meeting to-day, at which Said Pasha was again present, to discuss tfte Montenegrin question. Count Hartatehlt, the German Am- bassador, has been chosen by his colleaguas to conduct the negotiations with the Porte on this subject. Mr. •Kirhy Green, the English Consul at Scutari, will proceed to Cettringe. The Persian Consul at Jeddah has been ordered by his Government to deliver up the fugitive slave detained . by him. An English gunboat is expected at Jeddah. Thursday'isreports relating to the crisis in the Esst are very contradictory. One ...tit says "The Porte is resolved upon energetically carrying out the cession of Dub I cigno," and will, it is believed, v make essential sorters. @ions on the Greek question." A .111i-OffiCiAl Russian agency reports that "Eastern affairs continua to progress favourably towards a solution agreeing with the wish, n 1 the Powers." A third authority affirms that the Porte "is temporising on the Montenegrin question, and even contem- plates resistance." From • fourth source we learn that "new symptoms of hesitation have appeared." FRANCE. -

M. Gambetta was one of the guests at a luncheon given I by the Cherbourg Association of Commerce and hulumry Ito the Republican journalists on Monday. Replying to the I toast of his health, he said he had been reproached with having too great a liking for the army, but that liking was not in him dictated hoe warlike spirt, but by a desire to raise France to her former position in the world. though not by following a mere bloodthirsty ideal. "We wish." he added," to preserve in its present integritythat which remains to France, so that we may be able b. look forward in confi- dence to the Ware. and may at length learn whether justice exists here on the earth."

- - The Nark Luote Erpran, in its review of :he corn trade, saye:—Finer weather, with loft ahr. has enabled the farmers of the home 'awl Madmen counties to make a fair beginning of the harreSt. The wheat crop thm year will certainly be a great Improvement upon MA, hut the yield is likely to be one of the most uneven character. The markets of the pact week have been the subject of. slight retrograde movement, but trade real:tins no ausceptible to weather that the only statement that can be made with fair assurance of accuracy is that huyers will have the best of a market reached by • loug dusty road, and oellers the best of business ea a rainy day. Bell's ..If,s,rnyt,- rays ,—The accounts regarding nor wheat crops vary considerably. In some localities, with her weather, there will boa satisfactory yield but taken as a whole the crop will be deficient to a oonsiderable extent cotnpared with the average of seasons. Some wheat has been cut in several of the southern counties of England , during the past week, and it was expected that harvest week would have born g,meral in a few days, but there will probably be some hesitation about commencing, as the ' weather ia by no means propitious. It is to be feared that millers will not look with much favour upon the new wheat , when it arrives at market, as it will certainly contain too , much moisture to be profitably converted into flour. I Although some line weather is now very desirable, and, in- I deed, necessary, the rains have been of considerable ad- I vantage, and there is reason to hope that not only will there be a goal crop of barley, but that more and greases will be I abundant. The pasturee are full of feed, and the crop. of turnips and mangolds promise to be very abundant. Tbe potato crop is thus far mtisfactory, but there are indica- tions of dieeese, and it Is feared that if the present weather continues the crop will prove much less satisfactory than had been anticipated. Mr. J J. Mechi writes ,—" I regret to say that ftince nty last letter the farmers' prospects have very consider- ably darkened owing to an unseasonable July of Kill., weather, of tropical and cruAing cownpours, which have sopersaturated the soil, closing the gaping cracks, converting the lands into mud, and causing the under drains, where fortunately they exist, to discharge se though in winter: The fine an I promising crops of barley have been crushed to the ground, matted and twisted as though rolled, leaving erect temp of powerful weeds In many cams a second growth of gran barley is showing itself. The reheat crop, although less laid, is berOIT leg dark and raildewed, the grain swelling in it, c.tar by frequent soaking. The consequence is • delayed harvest and a much more costly one, for the reaping machine cannot, in many cases, be used. The labourers, knowing this and aceing the difficulty in movring or reaping, have increased their demands 20 her cent., and the farmers mnst pay it. Badly got hay, with warm and moist stacks, is too common. Let ur pray for the abeence of rain, with plenty of sunshine en mach depends on this Essex has suffered less from bed weather than many of the midland counties."

—Wegaraination of some forty reports just collected from various ports of America shows that the prospects of the wheat yield there are generally very good—in some cases excellent. Corn end ugs are very good, and more evenly promising. Potttaes with few exceptions, where the bug has been at work, promise very well. The fruit prospects . &revery good. ahnost without exception. The reports re- ' 'sting to the hay crop are not so satiefactory, with a few ex- ceptioos, hay grass has been light. In eonte parte of Canada la-mers have been hindered in their hay by wet weather, and it will lobe then, All their time to finish the housing before the wheat is ready to cut. It is uow tolerably certain that the crops in the United States, rams the New York Nation, will be unprecedented in amount. At the PrOduce Exchange there are those who calculate on a crop of 500.000,000 bushels of wheat, and 1,500.00,000 to 2,0m000,000 bushels of corn. . .

Unsettled and uncertain the weather continues to be, although during the past week the rainfall has been very moderate, and the temperature generally high. In twelve out of the forty English counties wheat harvest has commenced—these are Kent, Surrey, Sussex, Middlesex, Fasex, Suffolk, rilouteater, Dorset, I`.evon, Somerset, Hump- shire, and Wiltshire. A few wheat fields may have been cut in other counties, but if eo they are exceptional. In the west, midland, and eastern counties the wheat harvest as a rule is ten days behind time l north of the Trent it is decidedly backward, but with hot eunshine would come nearly up to an average date for the northern districts.— The Form,

-cre;prr.inilent write. as follows to a Manchester eon- temporary: *We have arrived at that season ot the year when under ordinary circumstances it ought to boa tolerably easy task to gaper approximately the yield of the trope. A month ago nearly everything was bright and the fanner was full of hope that, if he would not have first-clam crops, • turn at least had come in the tide which wae to repair hi, ehattered fortunes. But the storms of rain and thander which bare prevailed almost all over the country have cast • depressing gloom over him, and recently he has been look- ing with anything but satisfaction on the promise of the harvest. An examination of a large number of individual r, ports culled from ever, county is the kingdom giceesome ground for the farmer'. forebodings. From every quarter comes the cry of [wench wet. The ingatheriug of the hay has been a difficult task indeed. The math em counties do not appear to have fared so well as some of the northern districts in this respect In Pevonshire the hay harvest is 'till incomplete, and many of the counties between there and here are sadly behind. In addition to the delay in housing the bay, it is a light crop. In many place, the floods have spoiled the hay grass, and the stewing which the one grass has undergone is serioue. There is • greatly changed teen about wheat (since the late rainfalls. From many parts come cries of blight, mildew, and rest. In most places the plant is beaten down by the rains, and can- not now rise again, and the thin places which appearel to spring, and which looked some weeks ago like filling, look bad again. Barley and oats seem to he heavy everywhere, but they are badly beaten, and tangled, and twisted in stab a manner as to make it in many came impowdble to one the reaping machine, so that farmer, will have to fall back on the more expensive way of milting with the soothe. Pota- toes, which all along hare gii:en hopes of the beet crop within memory, will scarcely be at all disappointing in quantity, bat with a few exceptions the reports speak of the disease haying net in. The turnip crop is generally satisfactory. Mangels are variable, but scarcely so had as was feared some time back. There are good reports of the growth of the aftergrass where the bay has been cleared, and this under favourable circum- stances for rating, will be • great relief. Pastures too are reported to be very full of fond, and cattle are said generally to have yielded very well. The en- t few weeks will either add to the disasters of the British farmer or give him heart to battle in the future Fine dry weather euch as we have had iluring the present week can do much to repair the rate- chief which has been done, and a fiae autumn will enable the fanner to turn his fine crops of aftermath to the best so- coact, and so ahorten the winter. The farmers only hope is in the weather, and if that should be as favourable as it has been known during harvest and the back end of the yeas there le dill (mud for hope.'

THE TRAIN CAPSIZED.—THREE MEN KILLED. A terrible accident oceurre.l on Tuesday morning to the eapress Bans known as the Flying ncotchman, the swilteu train between London and Edinburgh. The disaster hap- pened within Wee mile. of Bernick. and it waa at that announced that the whole of the train had left the rads at a point known as Marshall's Meadows, where the is a rather sharp incline, and fallen down an emlankmeeL Happily, this report prored to be exaggerated, thongh the accident was found to Le of a very serious nature. The train which does not stop between Edinburg% and Berwick, left the former cite at 10-9, and consisted of engin, te.nder, van. two secord.cless carriages. one coniposite, and four first-class carriages. AU went well until the train reached a cutting near Marshall's Meadows, about 1115, when an axletree h 0!.,. out the engine left the rails. All the earriages toppled over, am! frightful conf u- eon followed. It was found that Join Thompsn, the engine driver, of Nearcaatle. and an extra auud named l'ieree killed. whilst the fireman namel Norman, was so 'seriously Injured that he died a few boors afterwards. A pawnor and the gaud, John -Turnbull. were ratler badly hurt, and some otbem received slight wounds. Fortunately the train was light for the rime of the year. The killed and hurt were at once conveyed to Berwick. It is said that the rails where the laident occurred had recontly been undergoing repair, , and that the danger signal was exhibited at the time. The nine o'clock express train from King's Cross had te atop Cl I Abbey Hill, and could not reach Edinburgh noah assistance was sent.

--1-TrlTng on Tueeday night a comma...lent fun. The exact cause of the accutent Is not known. The carriages fell in a heap &amine the wmt enihanktnent. Fortunately i another train was at hand containing two surgeon& ant • other medical men were forwarded horn Berwick by special train on soon ss news of the dimmer was receivrei. There co high bank on either Bid, of the crating. The engine now lies deeply embedded in the ground across the line, the tender lying on the opposite side. 20 yards up the bank. Part of the van lite 6,111 higher up completely smashed. Alongside of the van is one of the carriages 40 yards up the bank. Tbrm other carriageo lie along and across the line and another on the bank. The line M ploughed up in all directiots. All trains front the North ere brought round he , Sr. Boswells and Kelso. Turnbull, guard of train, woe sta.* !to be removed to his borne at Newcastle. Among the pas- sengers most injured is Captain Soutar, owner of the barque , Mersey, now Cl Berwick. lie jest Berwick Infirmary, and is expected to recover. Mr. Johnson fish curer, Moetrose, is injured, though not eminusly. Mr. Sharp, of Pneston,' Bournemouth, tool the King's Arms Motel, Berwick, but his ' injuries are not considered dangerous. From the fact that the accident occurred in • curve it is presumed that the I driver lid not see the danger signal n hieh seas ex hibited.l The fewness of the casualties ie attributed to the lent of the : train being light.

The engine land tender, which together weigh about 10 tons are both very greatly darnaged. A great part of the finer machinery ,of the engine seer. to have been destroyed ; while part of one side, near the driver's box, has been wrenched away, , and the funnel mai dome appear as if they had burrowed In the red clay of which the blokes.. ceinpoed. The sides of the tender were found battered in as if it had been a child's toy; and tlie van, which was thrown upon the top of it, was almost in splinters. No 2, which had both its ends teleecopel," wee crushed against the west hank, but had retained its perpenrlicul.it poeition, anti pavengers, if any were in the middle compartments, could have bad no difficulty in makiog their escape. From the east bank the engine and these four carriagm seemed Co lie in a eort of crescent form, with the lurns pointing to the east. The third and fourth carriage. , had been thrown en their Tide., and while the ends of No. 3 were battered in, No. I was a complete wreck, the roof being off, the rides driven in, and the framework wrenched away , from the body. Immediately after the amident, the ground around the carriages was found littered with luggage, cuehions, and splinters of the vehicles but the former articles were duly collected and carried up the hank. The fact that a number of the carriages had either luggage compartments or lavatories at both ends contributed not a little to the immunity Poen bodily Immo which so many of the pumengers enjoyed. Had the end compartments carried passengers these could hardly have escaped, as in the first six mrriages the eels were almom, if not altogether, des- troyed, arid the buffers of the carriages driven ri4ht through the woodwork. div.head: ANOTHER DREADFUL RAILWAY ACC I DENT. SIX KILLED AND TWENTY INJURED.
div.p: ANOTHER DREADFUL RAILWAY ACC I DENT. SIX KILLED AND TWENTY INJURED.

—• On Wedaeaday afternoon a terrible accident happened to a quick train between Leeds and Lancaster, no the Mitillolt Railway Company's link whereby PlI persinne ,'ere killed and over twenty seriously Injared. The train is said to have consisted of about eight carriage, and left Leeds .1 12 15, being due at Lancaster at 2 10. All went well with the train till it had paseed Wennington, about twelve mil. north of Lancaster, where the line becomes single, except at the Rations, where the lines are double for shunting purposes. The train waa not fixed to stop at Wennington. When it had got about three or four hundred yards on the south aide of the station, and was raking the facing point' to get on the single line, the engine struck the points, the weed of the train at that time being about 35 miles an hour. The engine ploughed along the line, dragging the car- riages along with it, till it came to a bridge which crones the railway, when the carriage next the engine caught the buttress of the bridge on the north side, and was smashed to atom.. The carriage following :t 'telescoped into Rand the remaining mrria ten were piled up , above them, and rested on the embankment by the side of the hridge. The engine was thrown somas the line, the , tender boing some diatance away from it. The rails were bent and twisted as though they had been piecescf wire, both lines were blocked. WAHILIAGTON CATHOLICS Awn run Sectroon Boost ' Movslirater.—at Ht. Mary's Catholic Church, on Sunday, the Bev. Father Foui, in the course of hie riermon, drew ; attention to the fact that A very large number of Catholic children were very irregular in their attendance at school. There wee no doubt, he said that the onus rested on the parents, and the mean. they were now taking in publicly noticing this matter wan in order that thorn parents would attend In their duty, which in incumbent on time., of making their children regularly attend school. 'Ph, reverend gentlenuin then read a lint of names, the Bret portion being of children who, during the present term, have not attended , halt the number of times they CoLthi, and the latter ponion being of children who, if they attend from this date to the • examination day, will Just manage to patio their requisite attendances ordered by Government. Father Pozzi earnestly entreated parents to be mors assiduone in the • performance of their duties regarding the education of their children, and referred to the recent meeting of the Town Council. He raid they had been threatened with the establishment of a School Hoard in Warrington but, happily, the danger had passed, and be hoped it would never again threnten. The School Board system of education had a Mrrible danger to Catholics. If the school, were to be placed under this law, religion would be entirely banished and nothing Int- a purely secular edu- cation would be given. Children would not receive any moral training, and they would grow up langerous poets to society. It was just the same with children, who were in the workhouse. In conclusion he raid that if the priest had the willing co-operation of the congregation they would have all the Catholic clindren attending their own echools, and would than remove tbe stigma which at present rests upon them, that out of the 1,000 children who were rambling about the streets, the greater portion were Catholic children. With generone help the new schools would soon be finished, and with increasnl accommodation there would he ample room for all, and with the efficient staff of teachers belonging to the school, a good sound prac- tical religious and secular education would be given, and this would be the greateg moment againet the establish- ment of a School Board in Warrington.

Tax Naw Latroa.—An improvement on the ordinary laugh has taken pines in the United States Thenew laugh, it is stated, is coming into general use this summer, and promises to not rely supersede the old one. To J•dge by the directions given to ladies in the OneiJenati Inquirer for laughing in the new style. the art in only to be acquired by some practice. the laugh goes like this—Te-he, te-he. ba, ha, ha! Oh-h•h-h—ha, ha, ha! A low. sly begin- . ning is made with the to-he, as though mirth were strug- gling inside:to break out through maidenly reserve, and the mouth is kept tightly closed. while the eyes are opened wide, thus giving an expreesion of mingled demureness and mischievousness. Then follows the ' Ha-ha-ha higher and louder, with a parting of the lips to show the teeth, if they he white and regular. The • Oh-h-h-h ' comes next in • tone of surprise, reproof, or artless gaiety, according to the nature of the thing laughed at, and the voice rises noon pretty little scream. The ensuing panne covers a sudden sense of the impropriety of making no ranch noise. The eyes are cast dcrwn, rind a bluah can in most instances be produced by holding the breath with the lungs fully in- fitted. The final ' Ha-ha-ha!' is given as a crescendo, spiritedly, and without any show of restraint, like the out- bursting hilarity of an unconventional milkmaid. This novelty in laughs is heard everywhere in the metropolis and is sore to become popular at the summer resorts. With • little alteration it can be made to to any mouth." We have not much occaeon for laughing no the Pm..nt moment on this side of the Atlantic, but to those who are in good spirits the new American laugh may perhaps be considved worth • trial.

THE RUNCORN COMMISSIONER-9 AND THEIR WAY OF TRAN,ACTING PUBLIC BUSINESS. Sir,—Accordrog to the report which appeared in your columns last Saturday, our miraculous Commiseionere have been again dietimaniehing theineelves. After a lull which hen lasted (unman months, they have once more broken out into bad graruniar and Billingleiste. The subject under die-1 mission was water, and the heat intralused into the debate was so intense that they very noon got into hot water. It Must have been a comical eight, end one which many people would have been delighted to witness I have no doubt ! that if many each entertainments are likely to take place, and the im6lic were admitted at a shilling a head, a good , thing could be roade of it, end the receipts might be reserved for the purpose of defraying the expense. of the Carious deputations which may from time to time be appointed to look after town's business at I.ndon, Paria, Now York, and elsewhere. No one would begrudge paying to see the per- formance. It must have been a sight worth seeing when Mr. Collier etruck an attitude, and. looking at the Chairmen,' scorned 6M authority. This reminds one of AjAI defying the lighting. Mr. Norman's determination to have his say in spite of all creation, in order to put him. self right with the ratepayer, was highly heroic: while lie. McDougall seems to have tern up and down, in season and out, and p ittering away without rhyme and rea- m., evidently with the intention of mystifying the Chair- man , but it VIM a ease of Greek meeting Greek. The little knot of ototructionista met with an ignominious defeat at the adjourned meeting. It would, perhaps., surprise those won- derful censors of the Bmrd of Commismoners to be Informed that the world would continue to revolve If they ceased to sit at that Board. It,. McDougall's constant reference to the dignity of the Board was fearfully wide of the mark, be- cause nothug is no lowering to the dignity of a public body as resisting the authority of the Chairman the members themselves have inatalled in office. lam sure the prevent Chairman acted with great forbearance, and showed .1 tho- ronghly gentlemanly behaviour, under pers..' attacks of the moat gratuitous kind, which would have driven almost anyone else frantic. Some months ago Dr. NlcDougall, I believe, proposed the adjournment of the Board for six months. lam halbinclined to the opinion that for once the doctor made a sensible remark. for the affairs of the town would not stiffer much if the Bawd were abolished, if such scenes as have taken place aro often repeated.—Your, &c, WALTER BUTT. Runcorn, Angnet 9, IMO.

Newrow.—On Tuesday last, about thirty ladies of the Earleetown Wesleyan Chapel, why have been working no nobly for the last twelve months for the above object, left, liarlestown station by the 2-35 train for Newton, and thence to explore the woods and places of interest on their way to I /esn Dam, the only obstacle beinga large gate to be climbed,' which is no easy task for ladies. The return journey was much pleasanter, and all reached Castle Hill. Newton Lake, in safety. Here a eplendid tea was provided by Mrs. Burdis, of Newton. Cloths were laid ou the grass, and all were ready to do duty under the presidency of Mm. Walker. After partakine of the good things provided, the company availed themselves of the pleasure boats, and, as the party kept well together some hearty singing was indulged In, which it characteristic of Methodists in general. This gave great pleasure to the fishermen and other visitors, all being I bent on enjoying themselvee.7 After a few remarks front the gentlemen present, a collection was made towards de- fraying expenses. The appeal was heartily responded to, i and remitted In a nice sum being handed over to the Treasurer. Sergeant Cummings sta.t that on the 3lst July the prisoner, in company with , his wife and son anti a lodger, who were then teeidents in Eirlestown, visited Mr. Barr's shop. Prisoner agreed to purchase a silver watch, valued at £5, and kis son a watch I worth about LA. The lodger alto purchased a silver guard, which, however, he changed for a more costly gold one. The terms of purchase in each case were that an instalment should be paid on the following day, and the remainder in weekly instalments. The jewellery was taken home by the parties, but on the following day none of the parties ela- neared with the instalment as prornised, and when Mr. Barr ascertained that the parties had left town, he obtained • warrant for their apprehension. The Bench held that the prisoner had been guilty of a breach of trust only, and that prosecutor's re edy was in the County Court. Prisoner was accordingly dismissed.

On Wednesday he commenced work at five 1 o'clock in the morning, and during the day he was noticed , by his fellow workman to drink a large quantity of cold ' water. About five in the afternoon he left his work, as his companions thought to obtain another drink of water, but not returning a search was instituted, which resulted in de- ceased being found lying qu'.te dead bmidc a coal wagon. CENTENARY CELEBRATION AT LYMM. The idea promulgated by the Sunday School Uniot of London at the beginning of this year of celebrating the ern- tenary of Sunday schools, as instituted by Robert Raikes, has of late borne much fruit, and the district of Lynne on Wedliesdey last showed their appreciation of the noblequali- ties of the Glouceeter journalist, and of his exercien of self- ! , devotion aud energy in eatablishing renvement of recognised benevelence, by haying 3 festival in his honour. The celebratisn was purely inaugurated by the dimenting portion of the district, as the Church clergy refused in absolute tern. to join in with the other bodies; but this, however, did not deter the Nonconformists, for the celebration may be said to have named off in a very euccessful manner. All , the arrangements of detail were ably carried out by a com- mittee coneisting of Mr. Everton (chairman), Mr. John Kneeler, Mr. .10110 Newburo, Mr. John Thomason, Mr. I Daniel 8r.y.1 (treasurer), and Mr. J. U. Ardern (secretary). , The festival took the forin of an open air demonstration, when the scholars front mch school in the village walked procemion. The day was enceettingly propitious for the event—in fact, the sun shone so powerfully that parasol. were ' in great request by the female., while the male portion bed to een eat and abide." It being the season usually celled "roshbearing," the village was quite refire, bunting being dieplayeal at various places, and everything partook Ifs gay appearance. In addition, the schools were all closed for the celebration, and the female population very gladly quitted the uncongenial atmosphere of the "cutting rooms" in order to partake of the festivities of the day. The echolars as- sembled at their respective echools at half-past one, and in processional order marched to the Cross—or as near to that venerable pile as the numerous collection of hobby berme, nutstalla arc, weed permit theni—wl eeeee under the leader- ship of Mr. N -wburn, they sang several hymns of a very in- spik ding nature, eccompanied by the members of the Lymm , brass bend, under the conductorship of Mr. Gregg. Of course, everybedy that walked nem in the gayest attire, and by some miracle or other every one had managed to become the possessor of a bouquet of flowers, which with the ! tasteful dresses of the females mode the ncene a remarkable one in point of contraat and colour. Each pemon was also provided with a centenary ineklal, which we understand were graluitously furnished by Mr. D. Boyd, the treasurer. After the singing of inn hymns, the scholars /darted on their pro- si al tour in the following order ' •—Weele an school, w ei'th'nabout 230 echolo., Zion Sunda'', school, with 120 scholars; Primitive Methodist school, with 120 scholars and the Congregational school and the Statham blission with 300 scholars. Headed by the band they proceeded through the lower part of the village to Booth's Hill, then by Church Green and back to the Cross. Halle were made at various places along the route, and singing indulged in. After the scholars had again been arrangekt near the Crone, the Rev. J. Bedell, pastor of the Congregational Church, epoke few words to them. Ile mid theynere holdingthet fentival because they loved to honour the man who first inetitutsid Sunday schools A liondrel years ego God put it into the heart of a man to try and elevate the social masees of the country, and he beg.in doing to by takieg children out of the strorte and teaching them to read and write and to grow up good men and women. Then began to spread the great work of Stinday ' schools throughout the land, and we who live in this the . hundredth ye kr of the establishment of Sunday schools had thought fit, op and down the country, to do honour to the illustrious founder of Sabbath schools. They were keeping it up thst day heartily, lovingly, and putilicly, so that every one could Ber bow happy they were together, and. nicking I all differences. wore all one in their praise to God that ever Sunday echools were inetituted. Ile hoped that might he ths first beginning of mine united gathering like that every . year. (Hear, hear.) Well, if they could not hold oneerery year they might manage a united gathering triennially, so ' that they might show the people that Sunday school , teachers, scholars. and friends could walk together, love one anethee, end encourage one another in their glorious and rend work. (Hear, hear.) Ile had greafly enjoyed being with them that afternoon, and Ike hoped that some time they might meet again in a aimilar manner to what they had done that afternoon and though they could not very well live ennther hundred years to have a feetival of that precise description, vet they might have united gatherings, like the one they had had Out afternoon. (Cheer. ) Another hymn having lean sung the scholars marche.l off to their different schools, where tea was provided for them. Subsequently all the scholar,. Adjourned sea geld at Foots Cray. kindly lent by Mr. IV flny.t. where gamer of all descriptions were indulged in until dunk. after which the band gave the lanai tinale and the celebration ended.

THE Boats. Mfix.—Mr. OSBORNE MORGAN, in moving the second reading of the Burials Bill, which leas already pissed the House of Lords, explained the previous attempts at legislation on the subject, and then detailed the provisions 1 of the measure, stating that the Government had not been able to accept the alteration made in the bill by the Upper Chamber, whereby, they had struck out the provisions abling Dissenters to perform service in consecrated ground, but had retained the provision enabling the clergy to perform I service in unconsecrated ground—Mr. 861111SFORD 130 PR, in moving the rejection of the bill, argued that the deeign of the Nonconformists, was to get poesession of the churches as well as the churchyards. He admitted the common law right of every parishioner to be buried in the parish churchyard, but he held that the clergy had no right to enforce the Church burial service in cases where it W. not desired. As the bill stood there eras nothing to pre- vent women from officiatingat funerals.—Mr. Warraa sup- ported the bill, arguing that the right of burial eras not only . a necessary beta civil right—Mr. S.M.. Latotrrow con- tended that no alteration of the law of burial would afford a just settlement of the question which did not give to all Her Majesty's subjects equal facilities of burial in all I the graveyards of the country. He admitted that the burial system required amendment, but maintained that the bill gave powers to Nonconformists In their burial grounds erhich it refused to the clergy of the English Church—The Hon. E. L. STANLEY thought the Government would bare done well to remember that there was. side to thin question besides the ecclesiastical difference, and that was the sant. tary side. He believed that no Burials Bill could be satis- factory which did not provide a public authority to control all the burial grounds of the country, and veg in some responsible body the charge of maintenance and, if need be, the extension of the burial grounds. But he could not help hoping that if the bill passed it would allay a good deal of the ecclesiastical !squabbling which stood in the way of a comprehensive settlement. In a few years' time, he be- lieved, everyone would feel that there bad been a fight about a matter which waa not worth fighting about. They heard a good deal about consecrated and unconse- crated ground, but they knew that when they went into a brand-new cemetery they did rot feel any reverence or awe for the soil and the prettily arranged walks and granite walls. It was the dead laid there which brought all the reverence they had for the ground.— Mr. MAKI. contended that the demand for the bill was not made by the bulk of the Nonconformists of the country, but bye motion of that body whom he termed the political Nonconformints.—Mr. It. Fowtan begged the House not to mix up the two questions of the right of burial and of die- establishment, and denied that there was any ulterior purpose in view on the part of the Nonconformists in the support they gave to this hilla He asked the Opposition at least to give the dissenters credit for being human, and not to believe that they were capable of creating scenes at the burial of their dead such as never had taken place in the past, and were not likely to take place in the future. Mr. Benton denied the assertion that no grievance had been shown, andquoted a series of statistics from the counties of Wades, showing that a large proportion of the Dissenters' chapels had no graveyards in which they could bury their dead. The figures proved that one of 1,979 chapels 1,424 were without burial grounds. The hardship was all the worm from the fact that Wales was a portion of the king- dom for which the Church of England had done less than it had done for any other part of the conatry. It had been argued that if the Dissenters got into the churchyard they would anon get into the church. Bet even if this hap- pened, where would be the harm ? It was not an uncom- mon thing en the continent for the members of two distinct seen to worship in the same church, but at different times and yet those sects continued to exist, and did not fight each other. It ems also said that possible, females might take part in the services at the graves of Dissenters, if this bill was passed. After further discussion the Hoene divided— For the second reading, 258, against it, 79.

. . - pleted hie forty dayw' bat at seen teaday. • largo mawsd preeent. At half-peet three Vele,k yesterday alrewoon, On. 'fanner's temperature was 99, pulse 82, respiration 13, and weight 122 the. His etrength, registered by the dynamometer, woe 78 kilogrammee in the right, and 72, left hand. The sphygmographic tracing. were regular and fair. He had several attache of mums. Dr. Tanner went out for • drive, during which he suffered from nausea md vomiting, nod he drank lye ounces of opting water, re- turning to the hall at halt-pant em,,. He walked op the stairs without amistance, and after walking about the room for some titne drank one ounce of water, which he ire- mediataly vomited. Al nine o'clock the doctor went to sleep, but, waking soon after, he had his bead sponged with cold water, after which he again fell asleep. It is estimated that 2,000 visitors called to eee Dr. Tanner during tbe day. The doctor,on the completion of hie 40 deye' fast, ate a peach and drank a glass of milli with evident relish; it wee tilled again and again, and was eagerly drunk by the famished men. He also freely indulged in water melons in the prmence of , about a them/end people, who repeatedly cheer d hint, It, subsequently waked down etairs without eminence, and drovein • coach to hie physician's residence, where he re- ceived eareful attenti.. He showed no nuns of diabase. At noon the doctor'a pules was 92, temperature 99 ,respiration 17, and weight 121 i pounds. Nzw Yuan, Sunday•—• London correspondent any. Dr. Tanner euccestfully completed Ida fast of forty days at noon yesterday. Elie conditi.- had not changed materially since the previous afternoon. The ball was deneely crowded with spectators, who were mad with curiosity and excitement. Dr. Tanner entreated them- to fall back and give him a chance to breathe, but the crowd pressed around him,, the hour of noon approached. When the deem whistle blew to denote that his fast was over, It,. Tanner jumped on a chair and swallowed a peach, notwithetanding the remonstrance of the watchers. The crowd cheered enthusiastically, and many epematore embraced him. Out side the ante-room Were 1,200 people, who greeted him with great cordiality. De. Tanner was thnn weighed, and found to scale 120 i lb. His pulse was 92, respiration 17. Descending from the scale, Dr. 'fanner immediately drank a glees of milk, and called for water mtlon. The ph yeicians remonstrated, but Dr. 'runner voreciousfy ate several alicos, rejecting the fib, and mellow- ing only the Mica. The physicians protested that he would kill himmlf, tun Dr. Tanner continued to eci the watermelon. Deriug the afternoon, he repeatedly ate alices of melon. After drinking on ounce of Hungarian wine, be ate Golf a pound of beafelmk, swallowing all but the Mugh parts. He , drank another ounce of wine, and followed this with a slice of melon. Then he ate su apple, and coiled for another steak, of which he ate bolt, pound. He then drank another ounce of wine. His nomach retaind all the foal that was taken, and It,. Tanner suffered no natmea. He appeared to be in excellent spirits, and add he felt capitally, and meld be ready for business by Monday. He retired at 11 o'clock, apparently out of danger. The physicians were utterly amaaed at the readiness with which his stomach digested the food. They had arranged a course of treatment, but Dr. Tanner took matters in his Own hands, and startled these with his imprudence. He ridiculed them, and said he suffered no injury. The total weight he had lost in the 40 dare is 381 b. The total quantity of water he drunk is 087} ounces. His respiration varied from thirteen to eighteen. His nanacttlar presente from one hundred and ninety-four to one hundred and dfty.eight. The temperatures show alight varietiona from the normal point. Practically there has been no fall whatever in the temperature despite the large waste of phosphates and the drain on the nervous acre to. /fie mind has remained clear and active. The toes of water , by the lunge was much lees than the minimum usually Oval hyphysiologiste. . •

A co;rceptindea writes t—Dr. Tanner dined on Saturday. His 40 daya'" fast " came to an end at noon, when he fared liberally, if not eumptucesly, on milk diet. In the United States, as M this country, great incredulity is expressed as to the genuine character of the feat, whiPt there is a general agreement that, even supposing the' fast" to have been accomplished, it was a foolhardy and utterly useless pro-1 eroding, partaking of the worst elements of the show business. A fastidg took has long been common among the Indian fakeens, some of whom • appear to abstain from food, and even to suspend animation, for much more ex- tended periods than forty days, and who do so under far stricter supervision than thst exercised over Or. Tanner, who, be it remembered, refused to agree to the conditione under which the regular medical practitioners of New York would alone consent to take part in the experiment. The circumstances under which the a fast "has been gone through leave as no proof whatever that the effort was honestly con. ceived and fairly accomplished ; and with this reflection the majority of people on both sides of the Atlantic will take no farther interest in the starvation theories cif Dr. Tanner. Dr. Tanner's fast is paralleled by that of a woman, Cicely Rjdgway, as recorded in judicial records. A writer in Soturday :tight, a forgotten magasine belonging to the early part of the present century, but full of curio°e matter, states that the circumstances of this fast are thus mentioned in "an old work containing the reports of many extraordinary trials." "In the 31st year of the reign Of that glorious Prince Edward tIl., and that of our Lord 1347, there was one Cicely de Ridgway, or Rygewa, indicted for the murder of her husband, but she refusing to plead and con- tinuing mute,notwithstandingall the arguments and threats the judges could use to her, they adjudged her at last to fast 40 days together in close prison without any meat or drink. This she actually did. For proof of this extraor- dinary abstinence I shell produce a translation of the record lodged in the Tower, which runs thus 'The King, to all bailiffs and others his liege subjects to whom thew presents shall come, do., greeting. Be it known unto you, that whereas Cecely, who was the wife of John Rygeway, wax lately indicted for the murder of the said John, her hus- band, and brought to her trial for the same before our beloved and faithful Henry Grove and his brother Judges at Nottingham, but that, continuing mute and refusing to plead to the same indicttnent, she was sentenced to be com- mitted to close custody, without any victuals or drink, for the space of forty days, which the miraculously, and even cootrary to the course of human nature, weut through, as we are well and fully assured from persona of undoubted credit. We do, therefore, for that reason and horn a prin- ciple of piety to the glory of God, and of the blessed Virgin His mother, by whom kis thought this miracle was wrought, out of oar special grace and favour, pardon the ceid Cecely from the further execution of the sentence upon her, and our will and pleasure is that she be freed from the said prison, and no further trouble given her upon the account , of the said sentence, dc.—ln wimps thereof, tic." .

The early history of Dr. Tanner has been" wrapped in, mystery." The New York paper., however, throw some light on the nate* of the doctor'. medical training awl pin- life. Ile came from England when a boy, and was working at carriage making, when it occurred to him to marry and start a greengrocer's bueiness—for, we presume, " greengrocer's shop is English for a "fruit store." Mr. and Mrs. Tanner neat betook themselves to medical studies', which they pursued in common; and at one time they were . joint proprietors of electro-therrnal baths. The pair were I separated tome years ago, apparently bc.cause Dr. Tanner became a bore with his theory that an empty ;date contained .as much dinner as a healthy subject requires. " Released from the healthy guidance " of Mrs Tanner, he began the experiments which have acquired for hini • fame that BO genius and few crimes could have won so rapidly. DR. TANNER'i Duesserr.—On Tuesday afternoon there was sent to Dr. Tanner, the great faster, a present of • box of honhoes, a pretty little enamelled affair not more than a linger in length, evenmetrically narrow, and very daintly ornamented. Within were a microscopic vial containing about 50 drops of Rolland gin, another labelled in printed let Mrs "claret :" two minute crackers split in the middle, so as to receive dainty morsels of smoked beef, and at the bottom half a dozen bonbons not larger than dried peas, and very tempting as they nestled upon the velvet lining of the casket. There was a eilver spoon, such as s fairy might . take tea with, and there were some dainty cups and mucera, bordered with cold. On the whole, it was a delicate piece of artistic workmanship. It came front a Canadian admirer. Tanner laughed heartily when the costly little souvenir seas ehown him.
